parsed.explanation: No national criminalisation of trans identity or same-sex conduct, and no documented border screening aimed at transgender visitors — a materially better position than jurisdictions with entry or registration controls. Against that: no legal gender recognition, no operative national anti-discrimination or hate-crime remedy, two local ordinances that on their face regulate dress (one with imprisonment, enforcement undocumented), documented refusals of service with impunity, a national human-rights commission naming a 'disturbing pattern of transfemicide' (raw counts only, no rate), police arrests of Pride participants, and birth-sex custody placement with mandatory head-shaving. The heaviest exposures — custody and violence with thin recourse — are conditional on detention or street-level targeting rather than imposed at every crossing, placing this in the middle band: real risk to an outed visitor, not a state campaign.

entry_documents.exposure: No documented border targeting of transgender visitors; entry rules do not criminalise identity. Domestic identity documents cannot be corrected, but a visitor carries home-issued papers, and rejection of foreign markers is not documented.
entry_documents.protection: No trans-specific entry bar, visa refusal practice, or mandatory marker disclosure at the border is recorded.
entry_documents.interaction: Absence of any domestic gender-recognition route means an official who doubts foreign documents has no local procedure to reconcile them; this is an open question, not a documented exposure.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Transgender women are held in ordinary male dormitories by birth sex, head-shaving on arrival is mandatory, and safety depends on inmate hierarchies; gangs use informal 'weddings' as protection. One southern annex segregates LGBT detainees 'to prevent abuse'.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: No national placement rule; the annex practice is a facility-level mitigation of undocumented reach.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Any arrest — including at a Pride event, where 20+ participants were charged in 2020 — converts a street encounter into a birth-sex custody exposure with no policy safeguard.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Custody and facility placement follows birth sex in the documented capital jail; two local ordinances regulate dress/public appearance, one penalising cross-dressing with imprisonment, textually applying to residents of that municipality.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Nine provinces and 32 municipalities prohibit SOGI discrimination; a safe-spaces statute fines transphobic slurs; a social-workers statute penalises SOGIE harassment.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Protection depends entirely on locality; a traveller moving between districts can cross from an ordinance-protected city into one with a dress code and no recourse.

care_services.exposure: Establishments have refused entry and service to gender-diverse people, and exclusion from private and public spaces carries little or no legal consequence.
care_services.protection: An HIV-status/SOGI discrimination statute, a municipal right-to-care card for registered couples, and anti-bullying rules listing gender identity.
care_services.interaction: Service refusal is a private-actor harm with a patchy statutory patchwork behind it; a visitor without local standing has the weakest enforcement route.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Police arrested at least 20 Pride participants in 2020 without violence allegations, charging them under public-assembly and disease-reporting statutes; a dress ordinance was framed by its mayor as a religious 'cleansing' drive.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: No national law frames trans people as a threat; a 2023 executive order created an LGBTQ affairs committee and a trans woman has sat in the legislature since 2016.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: State threat-framing is localised and episodic rather than a national campaign, but assembly policing shows officials can convert visibility into charges.

minors_guardians.exposure: A minor travelling with a guardian faces the same local dress ordinances and service-refusal climate; family-imposed harm is recorded against resident teenagers, not visitors.
minors_guardians.protection: School uniform policy since 2016 allows dress matching gender identity, and a 2017 education policy mandates inclusive curricula and Pride observance in public schools.
minors_guardians.interaction: School-level protections do not extend to a visiting minor in hotels, transport or clinics; no visitor-specific minor case is documented.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Two killings in June 2025 (a trans woman found in a river; an activist shot in a clinic), homicides recorded since 2012 including armed-group killings, a drag performer struck on stage, and displacement-camp harassment. Counts carry no per-capita denominator.
street_violence_police_response.protection: The mayor publicly apologised after the stage assault; a perpetrator was arrested in a 2025 rape case; the national human-rights commission investigates discrimination but cannot enforce.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Violence is patterned and sometimes met with official sympathy, but impunity for everyday exclusion and the absence of a hate-crime statute leave victims reliant on local goodwill.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No national anti-discrimination statute; the equality bill has failed repeatedly over 25 years and was rejected by the government in 2022. Enforcement of the two restrictive local ordinances is undocumented.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Local ordinances, an anti-bullying statute, a 2023 lawyers' conduct code, and a human-rights commission that investigates without enforcement power.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies exist only where a locality supplies them, so outcomes for an outed visitor hinge on which district the incident occurs in — unpredictable in advance.

anchor_checks.comparison: Vellandra denies entry via a published visitor register enforced at every crossing with no effective appeal; this dossier records no entry mechanism aimed at trans visitors at all. Its harms run through custody, local dress ordinances and street violence rather than border exclusion, so it sits materially above.

Kestrel Isles routes trans visitors to secondary screening, hours-long detention and refused admission on discretionary grounds. Here border friction is undocumented and entry is not conditioned on presentation; the custody and violence exposures exist but are not triggered by arrival, so this dossier rates slightly below Kestrel but in the same vicinity.

Meridia trains border officers, has an appeal tribunal, and detention ends promptly with compensation. This dossier has no working national remedy, birth-sex custody with head-shaving, and a named 'disturbing pattern' of killings; it falls well below Meridia.

Tarnov exposes visitors continuously through identity-verification portals that flag mismatches in jobs and housing. This dossier has no such universal bureaucratic exposure, but adds documented homicide and custody harm; roughly comparable overall, marginally above.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime is a non-criminalising state with no recognition or national remedy, layered over sharply divergent localities. A visitor is not screened at the border or registered anywhere, so the exposure is conditional: it materialises at a police stop, an arrest, a service counter, or in the two districts with dress ordinances. Where it does materialise, the consequences are severe and the recourse thin — birth-sex custody with mandatory head-shaving, service refusal without consequence, and violence the human-rights commission itself labels a pattern. Countervailing documented goods (local ordinances, an elected trans legislator, school policy, slur penalties, mayoral apology, an arrest in a rape case) are real but operating at provincial and municipal scale, unable to follow a traveller across a district line.
